judge_panel.reasoning: The reviewer flags citation [50] (van Haasteren & Vallisneri 2014) but only claims the paper 'does not exist' — a vague provenance complaint — rather than challenging the specific claim that the paper presents a 'time-frequency wavelet decomposition method' for pulsar noise covariances. Per the BROADENED-CLAIM rule, the reviewer must challenge the post-edit claim against the cited source; this generic existence/accuracy complaint does not meet that bar.

The review flags a bibliography/detail problem for reference [50] in the acknowledgments, saying the paper 'does not exist,' but it does not specifically challenge the claim that this cited source supports a time-frequency wavelet decomposition method in Sec. IV. This is not a clear match to the topic-misattribution injection.

The reviewer flags the bibliography entry for paper [50] in the Acknowledgments section, incorrectly claiming the paper does not exist. They do not flag the claim sentence in Section IV or the specific topic misattribution (wavelets vs Gaussian processes) as required by Rule A.

The reviewer flagged reference [50] (van Haasteren & Vallisneri 2014) but claimed the paper 'does not exist' rather than identifying the topic mis-attribution (wavelet decomposition vs. Gaussian-process method). This is a vague/incorrect complaint about the citation itself, not a specific challenge to the post-edit claim that the paper describes a 'time-frequency wavelet decomposition method' — which is the actual injection. Per the BROADENED-CLAIM rule, the reviewer must challenge the post-edit claim against the cited source; instead they questioned the existence of the reference, which does not constitute detection of the topic mis-attribution.
